title: A framework for improving urban soundscapes
central_proposition: This paper proposes a three-part framework, inspired by the Kano Model, to link urban design interventions to the perceived positivity of soundscapes, primarily mediated by user activity and stakeholder engagement, to guide assessment and improvement strategies.

concept_definitions.name: Soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: The auditory landscape, commonly known as the soundscape, which has many positive aspects beyond just noise levels.

concept_definitions.name: Positive Soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: A soundscape is considered positive if it enhances how people feel about the place.

concept_definitions.name: Kano Model
concept_definitions.definition: An approach traditionally used in product development to classify different types and levels of design choice or intervention based on customer satisfaction.

concept_definitions.name: Listening in search (analytical listening)
concept_definitions.definition: An active, conscious activity where the listener is 'tuned in' to whatever they are listening to, e.g., concentrating on birdsong.

concept_definitions.name: Listening in readiness
concept_definitions.definition: An intermediate type of listening where the listener's attention is ready to receive significant information but the focus of attention is directed elsewhere, e.g., recognising one's own phone ring.

concept_definitions.name: Background listening (distracted listening)
concept_definitions.definition: Where the listener is engaged in another activity, 'tuning out' the sound, e.g., concentrating on reading a book or holding a conversation.

concept_definitions.name: Basic (must-be) requirements (Kano)
concept_definitions.definition: Requirements whose absence leads to dissatisfaction, but whose presence does not increase satisfaction above neutral.

concept_definitions.name: Performance (satisfiers) requirements (Kano)
concept_definitions.definition: Requirements that behave one-dimensionally, where 'more is better' or 'less is better' directly correlates with satisfaction.

concept_definitions.name: Excitement (attractive) requirements (Kano)
concept_definitions.definition: Unexpected aspects of a product or service that delight a customer; their presence increases satisfaction, but their absence does not generate dissatisfaction.

argument_structure: The paper argues for a shift from noise reduction to positive soundscape design. It builds its argument by first defining the complex composition of a soundscape, then identifying the multi-faceted factors influencing its perception (activity, demographics, time, space). Finally, it integrates the Kano Model to classify stakeholder needs and guide intervention strategies, drawing parallels with automotive sound quality to suggest practical implementation.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The proposed causal logic is that urban design interventions modify the objective and spatial characteristics of a soundscape. This altered soundscape, in turn, influences how people perceive the space, with this perception being primarily mediated by their current activity and listening state. The Kano Model serves as a framework to understand how different types of interventions (addressing basic, performance, or excitement needs) will impact user satisfaction, depending on the stakeholder's level of engagement with the soundscape, ultimately aiming to enhance how people feel about the place.

findings.antecedent: Sound in public urban spaces (traditionally considered noise)
findings.mechanism: Soundscapes are multi-facetted and have positive aspects (e.g., soothing water, informative traffic sounds) beyond just negative noise levels. The perception is influenced by context and listener state.
findings.quote: Sound in public urban spaces is often considered in negative terms as both intrusive and undesirable... However, this issue is multi-facetted and goes much deeper than simply reducing levels. There are many positive aspects of a soundscape.

findings.antecedent: Design interventions (e.g., traffic layouts, acoustic barriers, water features) in a public space
findings.mechanism: Interventions directly change the sound field, affecting objective measures (dB(A), loudness, roughness) and spatial measures (mix, positioning, interplay of sources).
findings.quote: By making an intervention and consequently changing the space, the first effect will be a change in the soundscape itself.

findings.consequent: Perception of the space by users
findings.mechanism: For most users, the soundscape is an 'inconvenient and highly complex intermediate step' because their primary activity is not listening to the soundscape itself. Perception is influenced by the soundscape's effect on their activity.
findings.quote: for most users of a public space, their primary activity and interest is something other than listening to the soundscape.

findings.antecedent: Person's activity in a public space
findings.mechanism: Different activities (reading, conversing, shopping, sightseeing) lead to different 'states of listening' (listening in search, readiness, background listening), which in turn influence how the soundscape is perceived (e.g., annoying vs. interesting).
findings.quote: a person's perception of a soundscape depends most strongly on the activity they are doing at the time, and consequently their corresponding state of listening.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Truax [14] defined three states of listening.

findings.mechanism: The same sound characteristics can be perceived differently depending on the context (e.g., intruding on conversation vs. masking irritating sounds).
findings.quote: The sound of water, although sometimes considered pleasant, might become annoying if it is at such a level that it intrudes on a conversation or mobile phone call.

findings.antecedent: Listener demographics (age, gender, hearing impairment, resident/visitor status), cognitions (memories, ideas, feelings, attitudes, values, preferences, meanings, behavior, experience)
findings.mechanism: These individual differences and internal states shape how a person interprets and evaluates the auditory environment.
findings.quote: The perception of a soundscape is inherently personal and affected by what a listener, each with a unique set of experiences and preferences, brings to the listening situation.

findings.antecedent: Temporal conditions (time of day/week/year, seasonal differences, weather)
findings.mechanism: These factors influence the types of activities pursued in a space and the physical sound environment, thereby altering both the objective soundscape and its subjective perception.
findings.quote: perception of a soundscape may change over the course of a day, or over the course of a week or a year. Weekdays and weekends may produce very different soundscapes in the same space.

findings.antecedent: Type of space (public square, thoroughfare, shopping area), geography, culture, morphology, built landscape
findings.mechanism: These factors define the context and physical properties of the space, influencing both the sounds present and the activities that typically occur, thus shaping the soundscape and its perception.
findings.quote: The purpose of a specific type of space... will also obviously affect the soundscape, as will its geography, culture, morphology and the built landscape.

findings.antecedent: Level of stakeholder engagement with the soundscape (Noise Controller < User of the Space < Serious Listener)
findings.consequent: Type of soundscape requirements (Kano: Basic < Performance < Excitement)
findings.mechanism: Different stakeholders have different priorities and levels of direct interaction with the soundscape. Noise controllers focus on basic compliance, users on performance related to their activities, and serious listeners on excitement/cultural significance.
findings.quote: the requirements of the soundscape of a public space change from basic to performance to excitement as the level of engagement with the sounds increases

findings.mechanism: These are 'must-be' features (e.g., absence of nuisance, legal compliance). Their absence causes strong negative reactions, but their mere presence is expected and does not generate positive delight.
findings.quote: Basic or must-be requirements... Absence leads to dissatisfaction, but the presence of that attribute does not move satisfaction above neutral.

findings.mechanism: These are 'satisfiers' that behave dimensionally. Improving these features (e.g., sound quality that supports activity) directly increases satisfaction, and worsening them decreases it.
findings.quote: Performance – often called satisfiers. These requirements behave one dimensionally – a 'more is better' or 'less is better' mentality.

findings.mechanism: These are 'attractive' or 'delighters' – unexpected positive features (e.g., culturally significant sounds, sonic art). Their presence creates delight, but their absence is not noticed as a deficiency.
findings.quote: Excitement or attractive requirements – those, usually unexpected, aspects of a product or service that might delight a customer. Absence of them does not generate dissatisfaction, but their presence increases satisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Soundscape interventions (e.g., traffic, church bells, water features)
findings.consequent: Listener perception of calmness or vibrancy of the space
findings.mechanism: Interventions change the soundscape, which in turn affects the emotional dimensions (calmness, vibrancy) perceived by listeners.
findings.quote: introducing interventions such as traffic, church bells and water features into a soundscape could change listener perception of the calmness or vibrancy of the space.
findings.empirical_support_cited: [21] cited for a study by the authors.

findings.consequent: Health and wealth creation (e.g., reduced sleep/stress, increased vibrant feeling, attracting people to city centers)
findings.mechanism: Improved soundscapes reduce negative health impacts (stress, sleep disturbance) and can create positive economic benefits by making places more attractive.
findings.quote: The negative impacts of poor soundscapes on health are relatively well established... However, the concept of positive soundscapes... could lead to benefits for retailers and other businesses.
findings.empirical_support_cited: [28,29] cited for negative impacts, [30-32] for positive impacts.

findings.antecedent: Holistic consideration of environmental impacts (noise, air quality, safety, carbon emissions, soundscapes)
findings.consequent: Better planning decisions for urban interventions
findings.mechanism: Interventions often have multiple, sometimes conflicting, environmental impacts. Considering them together allows for balanced decisions that optimize across various factors rather than single-issue solutions.
findings.quote: Ideally we should be considering the impact of new transportation and infrastructure on noise, local air quality, safety and global carbon emissions all together.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The perceived positivity of a soundscape will vary significantly depending on the listener's activity, even if objective sound measures remain constant.
Interventions targeting 'basic' soundscape requirements (e.g., noise reduction to legal limits) will reduce dissatisfaction but not significantly increase overall satisfaction.
Interventions targeting 'performance' soundscape requirements (e.g., optimizing sound quality for specific activities) will lead to a linear increase in user satisfaction.
Interventions introducing 'excitement' soundscape features (e.g., unique sonic art) will increase user delight without causing dissatisfaction if absent.
The emotional dimensions of calmness and vibrancy, as measured by listening studies, will change predictably with specific soundscape interventions (e.g., traffic, water features).
The use of interactive soundscape simulation tools will improve decision-makers' ability to assess the likely impact of design interventions on perceived soundscape quality.
bridge_warrants: The framework explicitly draws parallels with automotive sound quality research, adapting its methods (target setting, benchmarking, perceptual dimensions, interactive simulation) to urban soundscapes, warranting the transfer of product development principles to environmental design.
The framework connects soundscape perception to health and wealth creation, warranting its integration into broader urban planning and policy discussions.
The framework acknowledges and builds upon previous soundscape frameworks focusing on sources, perception factors, and individual evaluation, integrating them into a more comprehensive model.
methodological_critiques: Traditional numerical signal metrics alone are insufficient to fully describe soundscapes, as they do not account for character or context.
Previous research attempting to classify positive soundscape features often combined descriptors of the soundscape, sounds, sources, and place, making consistent comparison difficult.
model_structure: The framework is structured in three parts: 1) Composition of the soundscape (Fig. 1), describing 'Sound' (objective measures) and 'Scape' (dynamic entity with multiple sources and spatial characteristics). 2) Factors affecting positive perception (Fig. 2), highlighting Activity, Demographics, Time, and Space as key influencers. 3) Application of the Kano Model (Fig. 6), mapping stakeholder engagement levels (Noise Controller, User of the Space, Serious Listener) to Kano requirements (Basic, Performance, Excitement), proposing that as engagement increases, the focus shifts from simple numerical measures to emotional dimensions and creativity.
limitations: Automotive sound quality is a simpler case than urban soundscapes, with simpler activities and clearer motivations for manufacturers.
Achieving similar accuracy for artificially created urban soundscapes as for interior vehicle sounds is not yet possible due to the large number of variables and time-varying nature.
Identifying key stakeholders in soundscape evaluation tools is not straightforward.
There is a long way to go before positive soundscapes are considered part of the normal planning and design process.
